summary: Artemis crews and robotic landers are heading to the Moon's south pole, where ridges decide when a site has sunlight for power and a view of Earth for radio. Ridgelight is a free web app that shows a site's real NASA LOLA terrain in 3D with the Sun and Earth over its horizon, for any date, and answers in plain words: Yes or Not yet, and for how long. It compares launch delays, ranks 14 polar sites for your dates and finds landing windows. Positions are checked against JPL Horizons. No login.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

You pick a lunar site (35 curated sites, or your own latitude and longitude) and a date. The app fills the screen with a 3D view of the site's real LOLA terrain, with a 120 km context tile around a finer 20 km tile. The Sun and Earth sit over the horizon, with thin lines for their paths over the next 30 days. A docked panel answers two questions in plain words: Sunlight for power? and Earth in view for radio? Each says Yes, Not yet or No, and how long until it changes. Power OK means at least half of the Sun's disk is above the horizon. Comms OK means the centre of Earth's disk is at least 0.5 degrees above it. A time dock shows three 30-day lanes (Sunlight, Earth in view, Both at once) and plays the sky forward. A Planner details tab gives elevation, visible disk and azimuth. A compare drawer holds up to four options with a delay of up to 60 days either way, and gives a one-line verdict. Rank sites ranks all 14 terrain sites for the same 30 days and warns when the top site has a long dark period, naming the best site with none. An Events tab lists every sunrise, sunset, Earth rise and Earth set in the 30 days, plus the start and end of each power and radio window. Select one to jump there. Triggers let you define conditions, such as sunlight for power and Earth in view for radio for at least N hours, with an optional minimum Sun or Earth height above the terrain. Matches are outlined on the time dock, saved in the share link and exportable to a calendar (.ics). Find a landing window searches up to a year ahead for the first windows that meet a trigger, and each can be shown or added to Compare. View from space zooms out from the site to the whole Moon, Earth and Sun at the same moment, with the real day and night line and Earth's phase; distances are compressed and labelled not to scale unless True scale is on. There is also a guided tour, a share link and a CSV export. All times are UTC.

THE PROBLEM

Near the south pole the Sun stays low, so terrain decides when a site has light. Earth also bobs near the horizon. Asking "what if the mission slips two weeks, and which nearby site has more sunlight?" is slow with map and ephemeris tools. Ridgelight answers it in a few clicks.

HOW IT WORKS

Sun and Earth positions are computed in the browser with astronomy-engine, on the Moon's mean-Earth frame, with no refraction. For 14 curated sites at or south of 80 degrees S, a Python build step casts 720 rays out to 300 km over NASA LOLA elevation data (5 m PGDA site tiles near the site, 80 m and 240 m polar grids beyond) and stores the horizon angle at each azimuth. A body is "up" when it is above that horizon. Windows come from a 10-minute scan refined to 1 minute. Other sites use a flat 0 degree horizon and the app says so.

VALIDATION

Positions were compared with airless JPL Horizons output at Apollo 11, Chandrayaan-3 and Connecting Ridge: 162 points. The largest elevation difference was 0.0063 degrees (0.38 arcminutes) and the largest azimuth difference times cos(elevation) was 0.0063 degrees, against a test tolerance of 0.05 degrees. Rise and set times were compared with a 10-minute Horizons table for March 2027 at Connecting Ridge and the Chandrayaan-3 Vikram site. The Sun at Vikram agreed within about 1 minute and Earth at Connecting Ridge within about 1.4 minutes. One Sun crossing at Connecting Ridge differed by about 23 minutes, because the Sun moved only 0.004 degrees per hour there. Illumination was cross-checked against Glaser et al. 2018 for 2017 to 2037 at 2 m: solar visibility 90.9% against 92.1% at Connecting Ridge (C1) and 88.8% against 89.4% at the Shackleton rim (S0). Nothing was tuned to match. Terrain horizons were checked with an independent re-run of the ray march.

LIMITS

Power OK and Comms OK are geometry rules, not power or link budgets. Terrain exists only for the 14 curated sites. Rays stop at 300 km or 75 degrees S. Near the poles a tiny angle error can shift a rise or set time by an hour or more. Triggers and searches are geometry only and look at most one year ahead. Landing-region coordinates are reference points, not landing points.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Mission planners can screen sites and dates quickly. Teachers and students can see why the south pole is hard, in plain words. Anyone can open it with no login. It works with a keyboard and a screen reader, never uses colour alone, and runs on a phone. The goal is a transparent, checkable tool that states its limits.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, three.js, Vite, Vitest, astronomy-engine, IBM Plex fonts, Python (numpy, rasterio, requests) for the terrain build. No backend: everything runs in the browser from small static files. Source code (MIT): https://github.com/ShehroseShabbir/lunar-landing-site-navigator-app

NEXT STEPS

Terrain horizons for any point near the pole, not only the 14 curated sites, computed in the browser from the LOLA grids. Rover and EVA route planning that keeps a crew in sunlight and in radio contact along a path. Permanently shadowed regions and their temperatures as a map layer. Simple power and link budgets on top of the geometry, for example the solar panel energy over a landing window. Updated site lists as Artemis and CLPS landing regions are refined.

USE OF AI

AI tools (Claude Code by Anthropic, run as several agents) helped with research, code, tests, review and documents. The idea, approach and decisions were the team's. Plain log for judges: https://github.com/ShehroseShabbir/lunar-landing-site-navigator-app/blob/main/AI-LOG.md
